chunks: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Qattan narrated that Abdul Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Hassani narrated that Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Hafs al-Khas'ami narrated that al-Hasan ibn al-Wahid narrated that Ahmad ibn al-Taghlabi narrated to him that Ahmad ibn al-Hamid narrated to him that Hafs ibn Mansur al-Attar narrated that Abu Sa'id al-Warraq, from his father, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather (peace be upon them all)

He said: When the matter of Abu Bakr came about, and the people pledged allegiance to him, and their treatment of Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) was as it was, Abu Bakr would constantly show him openness and friendliness, but see from him (Ali) withdrawal and reserve. This was hard on Abu Bakr, so he desired to meet him, to extract what was in his heart, and to apologize to him, when the people gathered around him and delegated the affair of the community to him, while he had little desire for it and was indifferent to it.

He came to him at a time of his distraction and asked for a private meeting, and said to him: 'By God, O Abu al-Hasan, this matter was not a compromise on my part, nor a desire for what I fell into, nor eagerness for it, nor trust in myself for what the community needs, nor strength on my part due to wealth, nor abundance of clan, nor taking it by force from others. Why do you harbor against me what I did not deserve from you, and show me dislike for what I have become, and look at me with the eye of disdain?'
He (Ali) said to him: 'Then what compelled you to it if you had no desire for it, no eagerness for it, and no trust in yourself to carry it out, and what need did you have for it?'
Abu Bakr said: 'I heard a hadith from the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family):
ai.seo_question: What was the theological and historical argument between Imam Ali and Abu Bakr regarding the legitimacy of the Caliphate?
ai.summary: This narrative from al-Khisal presents a structured theological argument where Imam Ali (AS) systematically refutes Abu Bakr’s claim of merit (istihqaq) based on the 'no misguidance' hadith by citing specific Quranic verses and unique virtues (fada'il) such as the Verse of Purification and Ghadir. The dialogue highlights the Shia perspective that Ali’s divine appointment superseded communal consensus, a conclusion validated by Abu Bakr’s dream but ultimately overturned by Umar’s political intervention, illustrating the tension between theological right and political reality.
